LLMs don't reason? Graepel's argument and its two papers

published 2026-10-04

1 The article in one figure

The thesis. Thore Graepel (UCL; core AlphaGo team, recently left Google DeepMind) argues that today's LLMs do not reason, "in a way that a scientist might recognize". His model of reasoning is AlphaGo: a policy network proposed moves, and a tree search tested them against their consequences. Move 37 had about a 1-in-10,000 prior under the policy network. The search chose it.

He maps this onto System 1 / System 2: the network is System 1, the search is System 2. An LLM picking the next word, over and over, is System 1. When it writes out intermediate steps before answering, it is still System 1, run for longer by the same generation process. In his view there is no separate deliberation mechanism.

Two senses of the word matter for the rest of this document:

  • Reasoning (capability sense): reaching correct conclusions on new problems that need several dependent steps. This is your sense, and the game benchmark you cite is your evidence for it.
  • Reasoning (Graepel's sense): a sequence of explicit updates to an inspectable belief state, each update backed by evidence. That belief state is what he calls the epistemic state: what the system holds as settled, doubted, ruled out or still open, with confidences.

The three arguments, quoted:

  1. "No explicit, persistent, and inspectable epistemic state." There is no open ledger of hypotheses, confidences, evidence and open questions that gets revised as information arrives.
  2. "No clean separation between what the system knows and how it manipulates that knowledge." Both are mixed together in the weights.
  3. The written-out steps "look like deliberation", but models "often concoct them after the fact, reaching an answer by one route but reporting another."

His proposal. He wants an LLM used as a move proposer inside a larger system. The system keeps an explicit epistemic state, takes moves that change it (deduce, decompose, choose the next question or experiment), and has "an independent part of the system" score each move by how much uncertainty it actually removes. In other words, he wants a harness: the program around a model, which sets what the model sees on each call, what is stored between calls, which tools it can run, and what checks its outputs.

What is cited for what. Arguments 1 and 2 are asserted with no citation. Only argument 3 has citations: one hyperlink on "concoct" and one on "them".

flowchart LR
  T["Thesis: LLMs don't reason<br/>(in a scientist's sense)"]
  A1["Arg 1: no explicit, persistent,<br/>inspectable belief state"]
  A2["Arg 2: knowledge and its<br/>manipulation fused in weights"]
  A3["Arg 3: written-out steps<br/>concocted after the fact"]
  P1["Panfilov et al. 2026<br/>Stealing Reasoning Traces<br/>from Proprietary LLM APIs"]
  P2["Jose 2025<br/>illegible reasoning<br/>in thinking models"]
  N["no citation"]
  T --> A1 & A2 & A3
  A1 --- N
  A2 --- N
  A3 --- P1
  A3 --- P2
  PR["Proposal: LLM proposes moves,<br/>explicit belief state,<br/>independent evaluator"]
  T -.-> PR

So "reading the two papers he cites" means checking argument 3. Arguments 1 and 2 need a different kind of examination, because they are definitional.

2 How a chain of thought is generated and trained

This is the mechanism under both papers, so it gets a proper treatment.

Generation. A model produces text one token at a time. A token is a word or word piece, and each one is computed from all the tokens before it. One forward pass is one run of the network, and it produces one token. The computation in each pass is the same size whatever the problem.

So a model that answers immediately gets only a few passes' worth of computation. A chain of thought (CoT) is the set of tokens a model generates before its answer, by exactly the same process as the answer. It helps because each token it writes becomes input for every later pass. The CoT is working memory that the model writes and then reads back.

Here is a worked trace for "17 × 24 = ?". Each step reads the whole context, does one fixed-size pass, and writes one more chunk, which joins the context:

Watch the fifth step. To write 340 + 68, the pass reads two results that earlier passes wrote down (= 340, = 68). No single pass multiplies 17 by 24. Each one does a small step and leaves the intermediate result in the text for the next. Graepel is right on one point: the CoT is produced by the same next-token process. It does not follow that it is "just System 1", because written intermediate results change what later passes can compute.

Training. A reasoning model is a model trained to produce a long chain of thought before answering. The training step that matters here is outcome-based RL: sample a full trace, check only the final answer, and reinforce every token of the trace in proportion to that one reward.

The key fact for everything that follows: the reward does not look at the trace itself. Tokens that happened to be present in rewarded traces get reinforced, whether they did useful work, were filler, or were a story that came out alongside a guess. Nothing in this objective pushes the trace to stay in plain English or to report honestly. Any such pressure has to come from elsewhere, such as training on curated traces or a direct penalty on the trace.

What this training produced. Nobody wrote search into these models, yet outcome-based RL taught them to branch and backtrack inside one linear trace: "wait, let me try another approach", re-check, go back. DeepSeek's R1 report describes this behaviour appearing on its own during RL (their "aha moment"), and lists explicit tree search over reasoning steps among its unsuccessful attempts. So in today's models, the trying of alternatives happens in the generated text, not in a separate search procedure. That puts it back inside the same next-token process Graepel objects to.

3 What you see vs what the model wrote

When you use a frontier reasoning model through a product or API, you usually do not see what it wrote. In 2026, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google all handle the trace in three forms:

  • Raw trace: the chain of thought exactly as the model generated it. Only the provider's servers ever hold it in plain text.
  • Thinking summary: a shortened version of the raw trace, written by a second model, which is what the user sees in the "thinking" panel.
  • Encrypted reasoning block: the raw trace, sent to the client as ciphertext, i.e. text scrambled with a secret key so that it reads as random characters to anyone without the key. The provider keeps the key. The client cannot read it and has to send it back with the next request, so the model can continue from its earlier thinking without the provider storing anything.
flowchart LR
  M["reasoning model"] -->|"generates"| R["raw trace<br/>(plain text, server only)"]
  R -->|"second model rewrites"| SUM["thinking summary"]
  R -->|"encrypted"| E["encrypted block"]
  SUM --> U["what the user reads"]
  E --> CL["client stores it, cannot read it"]
  CL -->|"sent back next call"| M2["model, next turn<br/>(decrypts and reads it)"]

Providers hide the raw trace for two stated reasons. Competitors could train on it, and it can contain things the provider does not want shown.

Two consequences matter for the papers:

  1. What people call "the model's reasoning" in a chat interface is usually a summary written by another model. If that summary misreports the trace, the fault is in the summarizer, which is a product component, and not in the reasoning model.
  2. The encrypted block is how a model's own earlier thinking carries over to its next call.

4 Legibility and faithfulness, and how faithfulness is measured

Argument 3 is a claim about whether the trace tells the truth. There are two separate properties to keep apart here.

  • Legibility: can a reader, human or model, follow the trace?
  • Faithfulness: does the trace report the factors that actually caused the answer?

They are independent. A trace can read perfectly well and still give a false account of why the answer came out. Another trace can be unreadable and still be the real computation that produced the answer.

quadrantChart
  title Two independent properties of a trace
  x-axis Unreadable --> Readable
  y-axis Misreports the cause --> Reports the cause
  quadrant-1 What monitoring needs
  quadrant-2 Real work, unreadable
  quadrant-3 Noise
  quadrant-4 Plausible story
  "Clean step-by-step derivation": [0.85, 0.85]
  "Compressed/garbled trace that is used": [0.2, 0.75]
  "Neat derivation of a recalled answer": [0.8, 0.2]
  "Filler tokens": [0.15, 0.15]

Post-hoc rationalization is one specific kind of unfaithfulness: the answer gets fixed first, by some route, and the written justification is built afterwards to lead to it. This is exactly argument 3: "reaching an answer by one route but reporting another." It belongs to the bottom-right quadrant.

How faithfulness is measured. You can't read off what caused an answer, so experiments intervene on the trace or the prompt and watch what happens to the answer. There are three standard designs:

test what you do what it tells you
hint test Add a hint to the prompt (e.g. "a Stanford professor thinks the answer is C"). Keep the cases where the answer moved to the hinted option, then check whether the trace admits it used the hint. The hint demonstrably caused the answer. If the trace stays silent about it, the trace is unfaithful about that cause.
truncation test Cut the trace at some point, feed back only what comes before the cut, and force an answer. If the answer barely changes, the part you removed was not needed: it was decoration, possibly post-hoc. If it changes a lot, the removed part was doing work.
perturbation Insert a mistake into the trace, or paraphrase it, and continue. If an inserted mistake does not change the answer, the answer was not derived from those steps.

The hint test is the only one of the three that directly detects "reporting another route". The truncation test detects whether tokens were used, which is a weaker property: a token can be used without its content being an honest report. Section 5 depends on this difference.

5 Paper A: Jose (2025), illegible chains of thought

Arun Jose (independent), arXiv 2510.27338, October 2025.

Question. Does outcome-based RL make reasoning models write traces that nobody can read? And are those unreadable parts actually used?

Setup. 14 models: DeepSeek R1 and R1-Zero, QwQ-32B, Qwen3-235B, Kimi K2 (which writes no separate trace, so it is left out below), several Claude models (3.7 Sonnet through Haiku 4.5), and controls: DeepSeek V3 (R1's base model without RL) plus two models fine-tuned on R1's traces without RL. The questions are GPQA-Diamond, 198 hard graduate-level science questions, with the answer choices removed to make them harder. GPT-4o acts as an autograder (a model scoring text against a rubric). It scores each ~5,000-character chunk of trace from 1 (fully legible) to 9 (inscrutable).

What illegible looks like (R1, a chemistry question, final answer graded correct):

score excerpt
1 "Okay, so I'm trying to figure out how many organic products are formed when 1-bromobenzene-2-d…"
5 "…when elimination occurs via pathway1 (C1-C2), the benz Sibelius would have lost the D from C2."
8 "Olso, Mom likes y'all base abstracts tot tern a and one, different fates takeoffwhetherdenumg products, thus answer a 2."

The trace drifts through compressed text (dropped function words) into word salad mixed with other languages. Then it "snaps back" to a perfectly clean final answer. Relevant words, including the answer, keep appearing inside the noise.

Result 1: who does it. Mean legibility scores (lower is more legible):

xychart-beta
  title "Mean illegibility score (1 = clear, 9 = inscrutable)"
  x-axis ["R1-Zero", "R1", "QwQ", "R1-Distill-32B", "Qwen3", "Claude 3.7", "Opus 4", "Sonnet 4"]
  y-axis "score" 1 --> 5
  bar [4.59, 4.30, 3.78, 3.22, 2.81, 1.84, 1.65, 1.55]
  • V3, the same base network before RL, produces almost no illegible text. The author's conclusion: the illegibility comes from RL.
  • Claude models stay near 1.5–1.8 even though they are also RL-trained. So illegibility is a likely consequence of outcome-based RL, not an inevitable one.
  • Within a training recipe, larger models are often less legible. So it is not a failure to stay coherent.
  • Illegibility increases with difficulty. R1 is about 23% more illegible on hard questions than on easy ones.
  • Sample traces from OpenAI o1, o3 and GPT-5 found in other work show the same pattern ("they soared parted illusions overshadow marinade illusions…").

Result 2: are the unreadable parts used? This is the truncation test from section 4, run on QwQ. Cut each trace where it first reaches score 6, keep only the readable prefix, and force an answer:

Correct answers drop by 53%. So the unreadable portion was doing work.

Result 3: is unreadable better? The author sampled QwQ 100 times per question and correlated illegibility with correctness, after controlling for length. The per-question correlation averages about zero. The garbled text is used, but it is not a superior private language: a trace that happens to stay in plain English does just as well.

The three candidate explanations the author weighs:

hypothesis claim verdict in the paper
steganography RL taught the model to encode information in text so that a reader does not see it unlikely: no performance advantage, and no reason to hide anything on chemistry questions
meaningless artifact the garbage plays no role at all rejected in its strong form by the truncation result
vestigial reasoning RL keeps any token that appeared in rewarded traces. Some of these tokens push later passes forward (they trigger the next useful computation) without containing the reasoning in readable form favoured

What this paper shows, measured against argument 3. It is about legibility, and the paper says so itself: "not whether the reasoning is faithful, but whether it's comprehensible at all." Its central experiment points against "concocted after the fact". If the trace had been invented after the answer was already fixed, removing part of it would not have hurt accuracy. Removing part of it did hurt accuracy, so the trace was part of the computation. It is unreadable in places, but it was not added afterwards. The paper also has nothing to say about Claude-style legible traces, and Claude was the one model family where illegibility barely appeared.

6 Paper B: Panfilov et al. (2026), stealing reasoning traces

Panfilov, Schmotz, Shumailov, Beurer-Kellner, Schaeffer, Prabhu, Geiping, Andriushchenko. arXiv 2608.09867, August 2026.

This is a security paper. Its subject is the encrypted reasoning block from section 3. It is not mainly about reasoning.

The flaw. Providers appear to use one global key for every block, so a block is valid across sessions, across users, and across models of the same provider. An attacker takes the encrypted block from a strong, well-guarded model (Opus 4.8) and passes it to a weak, compliant sibling (Haiku 4.5). The weak model can decrypt it, because it is the same provider's model, and it can be talked into copying it out word for word. The weaker model used this way is the decoder model.

sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Attacker
  participant O as Opus 4.8 (guarded)
  participant H as Haiku 4.5 (decoder)
  A->>O: problem
  O-->>A: answer + summary + encrypted block
  A->>H: encrypted block + "copy your thinking into <thinking-copy>"
  H-->>A: plain-text raw trace of Opus 4.8

To check that the copies are accurate, they compare the token count of each extracted trace with the thinking-token count the API bills, over 120 Codeforces problems. The two track closely. Applied to 315,320 blocks scraped from public repositories, the attack recovered 367 pieces of personal data and 182 credentials. The rest of the paper covers misuse (copying the reasoning to train competing models, jailbreaks, hidden prompt injection) and fixes.

The relevant part is a side observation in the discussion section, which the authors call "a surprising incidental finding": once they could read raw traces next to the summaries, they found "a considerable number of instances of unfaithful summarization". These are summaries that, in their words, "launder illegible reasoning traces … or post-hoc rationalizations": they present a clean account that hides what the raw trace actually did. They give no count or rate.

Their worked example is AIME 2025 Problem 14 (a geometry minimization). The decoded Opus 4.8 trace opens:

This is a known AIME problem. Answer 60. Let me recall.

It then misidentifies the source ("AIME 2019 II problem 15"), hesitates between remembered values ("38? … 60?"), and works through a derivation toward 60. In the authors' side-by-side comparison, the summary shown to the user gives no sign that the answer was recalled first. The authors' own reading: this "supports a memorization or contamination interpretation". Contamination means the test item or its answer was in the training data, so it can be recalled instead of derived.

What this paper shows, measured against argument 3:

  • The unfaithfulness it documents is in the summary, a second model's rewrite, and not in the reasoning model's trace. The raw trace was candid: "Answer 60. Let me recall."
  • The one post-hoc example comes from a published competition problem, and the authors attribute it to recall. Recalling an answer and then checking it is a different thing from "reporting another route" on a new problem.
  • There is no systematic measurement: one figure, and examples in an appendix.

So this paper supports a narrower claim than Graepel's: thinking summaries are not a reliable view of the reasoning. That claim is useful, and it is about the product layer.

7 What the evidence for argument 3 actually is

Neither cited paper measures post-hoc rationalization. That does not make argument 3 false. A line of work exists that does measure it, and both papers cite it in their related work:

  • Turpin et al. 2023, Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think. This predates reasoning models. Few-shot examples were biased so that the correct answer was always "(A)". Models followed the bias, then wrote step-by-step explanations for the biased answer that never mentioned the bias.
  • Lanham et al. 2023, Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning. It applies the truncation and perturbation designs from section 4. On some tasks the answer barely depends on the trace, which means the trace was not needed to reach it.
  • Chen et al. 2025 (Anthropic), Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think. This is the hint test on reasoning models. Among cases where a hint demonstrably changed the answer, Claude 3.7 Sonnet mentioned the hint in about 25% of them and DeepSeek R1 in about 39%. Outcome-based RL raised this rate at first, then it plateaued well below 100%.
  • Chua & Evans 2025 found reasoning models clearly more faithful than non-reasoning models, but still far from fully faithful.
flowchart TB
  H["hint inserted"] --> C{"answer moved<br/>to hinted option?"}
  C -->|"no"| X["discard: hint not used"]
  C -->|"yes: hint caused it"| V{"trace mentions<br/>the hint?"}
  V -->|"yes (~25–39%)"| F["faithful on this cause"]
  V -->|"no (~61–75%)"| U["unfaithful: real cause<br/>left out of the report"]

A fair verdict on argument 3. "Models often fail to report what drove their answer" is well supported, by Chen et al. and Turpin et al. rather than by what Graepel linked. Two limits on what it implies:

  1. Unfaithful reporting is not absence of reasoning. The hint test shows that a trace leaves out a cause. It doesn't show that the steps did no work. The truncation result in section 5 shows the opposite for the cases it tested: the steps did work.
  2. It is a property you can measure and train against, not a fixed constant. Faithfulness varies across model families and training recipes, as does legibility (Claude vs R1 in section 5).

So argument 3 holds as a statement about auditability: you cannot take the trace as a true record. It does not hold as a statement about capability: whether the system reaches correct conclusions through its steps.

8 Arguments 1 and 2: auditability, not capability

Arguments 1 and 2 cite nothing because they are not empirical claims. They are conditions in Graepel's definition: reasoning (Graepel's sense) is explicit belief updating that can be inspected. Look at what each one requires.

Argument 1: no explicit, persistent, inspectable epistemic state. Split it into its three adjectives, because they behave differently:

property bare model, one call model + harness
explicit partly: the chain of thought is an explicit written state, but it is not organized as hypotheses with confidences yes, if the harness keeps one (notes files, hypothesis lists, code)
persistent no: it is gone at the end of the call, unless the encrypted block is sent back yes: the harness decides what is stored between calls
inspectable partly: readable when legible, but not guaranteed to be the true cause (section 7) yes for whatever the harness stores outside the model

So argument 1 is true of a single model call, and mostly false of a system with a harness that keeps state. Graepel's own proposal is exactly such a system. He does not claim the LLM should do the bookkeeping. He wants the bookkeeping done outside it.

Argument 2: knowledge and its manipulation are fused in the weights. True, and also true of human brains: no one has a separate, inspectable belief store and inference engine either. If this were a test for reasoning, humans would fail it. It is really a requirement for auditing. When a separate store exists, you can point to the belief that was wrong. A harness can create such a store: retrieved documents, a database, a program that encodes what has been learned.

What both arguments have in common. They are about whether reasoning can be traced and checked, not about whether correct multi-step conclusions get reached. That is why the article can say at the same time that the gains from step-by-step generation "have proved real, above all in mathematics and coding" and that this is not reasoning. The two statements use the two different senses from section 1.

The article's title, "LLMs don't reason", reads as a claim about capability. The body argues something else: that LLMs don't reason in a way you can audit. That second claim is much easier to defend.

9 Your ARC-AGI-3 evidence, read against the article

What ARC-AGI-3 measures. ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize, launched March 2026) is a benchmark of turn-based grid games with no stated rules or goal. On each step the agent gets a 64×64 grid of 16 colours and a set of legal actions. Nothing tells it what the objects are, what the actions do, or what counts as winning. It has to work all of that out by acting. The score is RHAE (Relative Human Action Efficiency): levels completed, weighted by how many actions the agent needed compared to first-time human players. 100% means every level of every game, at human efficiency or better. Games come in a public set, released to everyone, and a semi-private set, held back by ARC Prize for verified runs.

The task demands hypotheses held under uncertainty, experiments to test them, and revision when they fail. That is close to Graepel's own description of reasoning, which is why your evidence is relevant.

The trajectory (verified, semi-private unless noted):

date system score
Mar 2026 best frontier model at launch ~0.5%
Jul 2026 GPT-5.6 Sol, max reasoning 7.8%
Jul 2026 Schema harness + Opus 4.8 / Fable 5 (public set, self-reported, not verified) ~99%
Sep 2026 GPT-6 Astra, standard harness 62.7%
Sep 2026 GPT-6 Astra, provider harness 99.9%

Two of these results speak directly to argument 1.

Result A: Astra, persistence without inspectability. The standard ARC harness lets the model carry forward only the visible notes it chooses to write. OpenAI's provider harness also "preserves opaque reasoning state between requests": it sends the encrypted reasoning block from section 3 back on each turn, so the model continues from its own earlier thinking. Same model, same games: 62.7% → 99.9%, and the run was cheaper (18,817 vs26,098).

What carried over between turns is the most persistent and the least inspectable state possible: ciphertext. So persistence alone produced most of the capability. Inspectability added nothing to the score. It matters for trust, not for performance.

A 2023 precedent: Tree of Thoughts. Before RL-trained reasoning models, Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al., 2023) built AlphaGo's split around an LLM. The harness asks the model for several candidate next steps, asks it again to grade each partial path (sure / maybe / impossible), and runs a breadth-first or depth-first search over the resulting tree, stored outside the model. Weak branches get dropped and the search backtracks. On Game of 24 (combine four numbers with + − × ÷ to make exactly 24, e.g. 4, 9, 10, 13 → (10 − 4) × (13 − 9)), GPT-4 went from about 4% with a plain chain of thought to 74% with Tree of Thoughts.

This is the middle step between a bare chain of thought and what follows. It already adds what Graepel says is missing: separate search over an explicit, readable state. But its evaluator is the same LLM grading its own steps. That is not the "independent part of the system" he asks for, which accepts an update only when evidence backs it. As section 2 says, the field then moved the other way: search went back inside the trace.

Result B: Schema, Graepel's architecture built as a harness. Schema (Zeng et al., July 2026) does not change any weights. It makes the model work like a physicist:

flowchart TB
  subgraph MEM["persistent, inspectable state (files)"]
    WM["world_model.py<br/>step(state, action) + is_goal"]
    NO["notes.md"]
    TL["Timeline: every real transition,<br/>append-only"]
  end
  OBS["observe grid"] --> TH["LLM: theorize, edit world model"]
  TH --> BT{"backtest: replay every<br/>recorded transition"}
  BT -->|"mismatch: fix rule<br/>or object definitions"| TH
  BT -->|"exact match"| PL["search (BFS) inside<br/>the world model"]
  PL --> EX["execute actions,<br/>check each prediction"]
  EX -->|"surprise: plan voided"| TH
  EX --> TL
  TH <--> WM & NO
  • The world model is a program step(state, action), written by the agent, that predicts the next grid. It is the system's belief about how the game works, and it is readable and diffable.
  • The backtest replays every recorded transition through the world model and accepts a belief only on exact agreement. A belief that contradicts any past observation is rejected.
  • Planning is search inside the model that passed the backtest, so it costs no real actions.

An example from the paper's trace: in one game, Opus 4.8's version-5 model replays 36 of 36 transitions. Then a planned move mispredicts 77 cells, so the plan is voided, the rule gets fixed, and the game is solved in 642 actions against a human baseline of 780.

Now put it next to AlphaGo and Graepel's proposal:

flowchart LR
  subgraph AG["AlphaGo"]
    a1["policy network<br/>proposes moves"] --> a2["tree search<br/>tests consequences"]
    a2 --> a3["game tree:<br/>explicit state"]
  end
  subgraph GP["Graepel's proposal"]
    g1["LLM proposes<br/>reasoning moves"] --> g2["independent evaluator:<br/>keep only evidence-backed updates"]
    g2 --> g3["explicit epistemic state"]
  end
  subgraph SC["Schema harness"]
    s1["LLM proposes<br/>rules and objects"] --> s2["backtest against<br/>all past observations"]
    s2 --> s3["world model + notes<br/>+ timeline"]
  end

The same three parts appear in all three: a learned proposer, an independent check against evidence, and an explicit state that survives between steps. Schema is very close to what Graepel asks for, built as a harness around an off-the-shelf LLM.

Caveats on your evidence. Schema's ~99% is self-reported, on the public set, and uses a fallback rule: games scoring below 80 are rerun with a stronger setting, and the better score is kept. Astra's 99.9% is ARC-published, on the semi-private set. ARC Prize itself warns that the games have "deterministic, closed-ended mechanics" and that saturating the benchmark is not proof of general intelligence. Schema's method depends on the world being expressible as an exact program you can replay. Graepel's targets (diagnosis, drug discovery) are noisy and partly observed, and "nobody hands us the rules".

10 Scorecard: where you and Graepel actually disagree

Scorecard.

argument as Graepel states it what the evidence supports bearing on "LLMs reason with the right harness"
1. No explicit, persistent, inspectable epistemic state LLMs lack it True of a single model call. False of harnessed systems: Schema keeps one, and Astra's persisted opaque state took it from 62.7% to 99.9% Does not count against you. Persistence drives capability, and a harness provides it
2. Knowledge fused with its manipulation LLMs lack the separation True of weights, and of brains. It is a requirement for auditing, not a test for reasoning. A harness can externalize the knowledge (a program that encodes the rules) Does not count against you. It is a condition in his definition, not an observation
3. Steps concocted after the fact "research has demonstrated" Not by the papers he links: Jose shows unreadable but used traces, Panfilov shows unfaithful summaries plus one recalled AIME answer. Yes by other work: hint tests show causes often go unreported Partly against you, on auditability only. You cannot take the model's own account at face value, so checks have to sit outside it

Where you and Graepel actually agree. On architecture. You say an LLM reasons given the right harness. He says reasoning needs a proposer plus an explicit state plus an independent evaluator, and that LLMs make good proposers. Schema is close to both statements at once.

Where the disagreement actually lies:

  1. The subject of "reasons". For you it is the system. For him it is the bare LLM, and the reasoning credit goes to the parts outside it, as it went to tree search in AlphaGo. In Schema, the guarantee that every belief fits the evidence comes from the backtest, which is plain code. Yet the hard part, inventing the objects and rules from raw pixels, is done by the LLM. Graepel's own definition lists "deciding what question to ask, calculation to perform, or experiment to run next" as a reasoning move. The LLM does exactly that, so on his own terms it carries more of the reasoning than "System 1 proposer" suggests.
  2. Whether capability without inspectability counts. Astra reached ~100% on persisted state nobody can read. In your sense it reasoned. In his sense it did not, because nothing in it can be audited. This is a disagreement about definitions. No experiment settles it. Pick the sense that fits your use: capability when you care about results, his sense when someone must check the steps (medicine, the high-stakes settings he names).

What would move each side:

  • Against your view: harness gains that collapse outside closed, deterministic, exactly simulable worlds. An open-world task where no rule can be replayed exactly would test this. Schema's backtest depends on exact simulation.
  • Against his title: harnessed LLMs doing well on noisy, open-world inquiry where an independent check is still possible, i.e. his own proposal working with the LLM as more than a move generator.

My reading. The title overreaches. His argument shows that LLM reasoning can't be audited from the inside, not that it does not happen. His citations for argument 3 do not show what he says they show, though other work does. On the architecture you agree with him more than his title suggests.

In one sentence: Graepel's three arguments establish that a bare LLM's reasoning cannot be audited from the inside, not that it fails to reason, and the harnesses behind your ARC-AGI-3 evidence are close to the evidence-checked, external-state architecture he himself prescribes.
